title: Ζεὺς καὶ ὄφις
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 122 (= Perry 221). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Τοῦ Διὸς γάμους ποιοῦντος, πάντα τὰ ζῷα ἤνεγκαν δῶρα, ἕκαστον κατὰ τὴν οἰκείαν δύναμιν.
sentences.tr: Tou Dios gamous poiountos, panta ta zōia ēnenkan dōra, hekaston kata tēn oikeian dynamin.
sentences.l: When Zeus was making his wedding, all the animals brought gifts, each according to its own power.
sentences.n: γάμους ποιεῖν is the regular idiom for celebrating a wedding, plural because the Greek wedding is a run of rites over days. Genitive absolute again for the setting. οἰκεῖος is what belongs to one's own house, hence one's own means.

sentences.t: Ὄφις δὲ ἕρπων ῥόδον λαβὼν ἐν τῷ στόματι ἀνέβη.
sentences.tr: Ophis de herpōn rhodon labōn en tōi stomati anebē.
sentences.l: But a snake, creeping, having taken a rose in its mouth, went up.
sentences.i: But a snake came creeping up with a rose held in its mouth.
sentences.n: ἀνέβη, 'went up', because the wedding is on Olympus and everything else must climb to it — which for a creature that ἕρπει, that goes on its belly, is already part of the picture. Initial ῥ is written rh in the romanization: the rough breathing sits on it.

sentences.t: Ἰδὼν δὲ αὐτὸν ὁ Ζεὺς ἔφη· « Τῶν ἄλλων πάντων τὰ δῶρα λαμβάνω, ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ σοῦ στόματος λαμβάνω οὐδ’ ὅλως. »
sentences.tr: Idōn de auton ho Zeus ephē· « Tōn allōn pantōn ta dōra lambanō, apo de tou sou stomatos lambanō oud’ holōs. »
sentences.l: And Zeus, seeing him, said: « Of all the others I take the gifts, but from your mouth I take nothing at all. »
sentences.n: λαμβάνω is repeated on either side of the δέ, the acceptance set against the refusal in the same word. ὅλως with a negative is 'not in the least'. The refusal turns on the mouth, not the rose: the gift is beautiful and the vessel is venomous.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι τῶν πονηρῶν αἱ χάριτες φοβεραί εἰσιν.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti tōn ponērōn hai charites phoberai eisin.
sentences.l: The fable shows that the favours of the wicked are to be feared.
sentences.n: χάρις is both the kindness done and the gratitude owed for it; here it is the good turn offered. φοβερός looks active but regularly means 'such as to inspire fear', a thing one has cause to dread.
